# Portraits and sculptures open EAFIT's exhibitions in 2016

**The University will inaugurate its first art exhibition of the year this Thursday, March 17, at 6:30 pm, in the Arts Center.**

**The featured artist is Gustavo Jaramillo V., who will be exhibiting drawings and sculptures of prominent figures.**

- [Start](https://www.eafit.edu.co/)
- [News](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias)
- [Our Talent Community](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias/nuestra-comunidad-de-talento)
- Portraits and Sculptures Open EAFIT's 2016 Exhibitions

![Image: Portraits and sculptures opens EAFIT's exhibitions in 2016](https://universidadeafit.widen.net/content/514dee47-ff46-4105-9a1a-87a9805ca44f/web/mar14.jpg?crop=yes&k=c&w=823&h=450&itok=aYm_GhY0)

Stories and Sculptures is the exhibition that will be open until the first week of May. The entire academic community and the city at large are invited to visit it free of charge. Pictured is Dinah Washington.

An exhibition that brings together portraits of passionate figures who have influenced the history of humanity, with allegorical sculptures that reflect ideas and fears. This is the proposal of the draftsman, painter, and sculptor Gustavo Jaramillo V., the protagonist of the exhibition that inaugurates EAFIT's 2016 exhibition series.

This is Portraits and Sculptures, an exhibition that will be on display with free admission at the Arts Center of the Luis Echavarría Villegas Cultural Center Library of the University, from this Thursday, March 17, until the first week of May.

The artist will exhibit approximately 72 pencil drawings that, as explained by Sol Astrid Giraldo Escobar, author of the exhibition's curatorial texts, reflect the personalities and values ​​of the figures depicted. The individuals in Jaramillo's portfolio come from the fields of music, painting, and writing, and are, for him, legends whose actions and ideas have shaped the culture of the last 150 years.

The drawings are divided into series, each featuring figures who may never have met but whose shared characteristics offer much to discuss. International and national figures such as Claude Monet, Pablo Picasso, Friedrich Nietzsche, Gabriel García Márquez, and Carlos Gaviria are among those whose faces will be seen in the exhibition, which will also include a series dedicated to prominent Colombian intellectuals.

In addition to the portraits, the exhibition will include a room dedicated to sculptures that, according to Sol Giraldo, demonstrate Gustavo Jaramillo's interpretation of feelings and ideas such as indifference, death, and violence.

Having works like Portraits and Sculptures is important for EAFIT because it fulfills the objective of valuing the works of national artists who, although they have a very good career, need to be collected to look at themselves again, analyze and review their contributions to culture.

That is why Juan Antonio Agudelo Vásquez, coordinator of the Cultural Extension Area of ​​EAFIT, invites the entire city to "share the experience of having the perfection of these portraits, of the play of light and shadows that will be prodigiously reflected in each of the faces and sculptures."

###### An artist from Antioquia who revives history

Sociologist, painter, sculptor and draftsman are the facets of Gustavo Jaramillo, a Colombian artist who was born in Medellín in 1948 and has dedicated himself, among many things, to reviewing and studying characters who according to him have marked the history of humanity.

After completing his sociology studies, he traveled to San Francisco, New York, and Milan to study the lost-wax casting technique in bronze sculpture. His portraits and sculptures are held in private collections in Medellín, Cali, Bogotá, Caracas, San Francisco, Rome, and Milan. From 2004 to 2006, he served as Consul General of the Republic of Colombia in Milan, Italy.

The techniques he uses in his works are pencil drawing on paper; pencil drawing with turpentine on paper; oil pastel on paper; oil on paper; and sculpture in bronze, wax, and resin

Sol Astrid Giraldo considers him an artist who likes to keep a low profile, who has always worked independently, very much alone, but constantly creating works.

This is one of the reasons why Giraldo also finds it interesting that the University collects his works, in order to promote the appreciation of art in the region by the general community.
